new_statements.quote: In Kulango tone is confined to a grammatical function on verbs; it is not a lexical marker.
new_statements.citation: Micheli, Ilaria (2017). Son of the root. Djedwa Yao Kuman, Kulango healer and hunter (transl. Mark Brady). Trieste: EUT, ATrA 2. 298 pp. Open access, IRIS Trieste handle 11368/2893525.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. (298 pp., text layer; extracted text). PDF page 13 = printed p. 13 ('introduction 13' footer), footnote 4 reads exactly: "In Kulango tone is confined to a grammatical function on verbs; it is not a lexical marker." Verbatim. It is a footnote to a sentence about Abron talking drums; the surrounding section is the ethnographic introduction, not a phonology section. The only other prosodic material in the book is in text-notes on verbal tone patterns (imperative = pronoun + high tone + verb + high tone, Micheli 2007: 78-79; injunctive/negative tonal structures with an M tone and end-phrase downdrift, Micheli 2007: 85). a full-text search for stress/accent the f…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand prosodic statement opened says Kulango (Nassian dialect) uses tone, but only grammatically on verbs (e.g. imperative/injunctive/negation tonal patterns, cross-referenced to Micheli 2007: 78-79, 85), not as a lexical contrast. Nothing is said about word stress or accent placement. For Bouna proper, PHOIBLE (from Elders 2008) reports two level tones (H, L), second-hand; Fiorio's review of Micheli 2007 reports three distinctive tones for Nassian.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about tone on verbs in connected speech/texts; no word-level stress domain is discussed. It describes the Nassian dialect, which Glottolog files as nass1235 under Bondoukou Kulango (bond1246), not under boun1243.
new_statements.identity_note: The one first-hand statement opened (Micheli 2017, p.13 fn 4) describes the Nassian dialect, which Glottolog 5.x files as nass1235 under Bondoukou Kulango (bond1246), not under boun1243; Micheli (2017: 11 fn 1) notes Ethnologue maps Nassian into the Bouna variant but she considers it closer to Bondoukou on morphological grounds. Kra's Corela papers describe Tanda (also bond1246). Nothing opened describes Bouna proper (boun1243); its only descriptions, Elders 2008 and Prost 1974, are print-only.

sources.note: Nassian dialect (Glottolog nass1235 under bond1246). p.13 fn 4: 'In Kulango tone is confined to a grammatical function on verbs; it is not a lexical marker.'
